subject: AI safety is on the Trump-Xi agenda. Chips are not.
bodyMarkdown:
Trump hosts Xi Jinping in Washington on Thursday, and for the first time AI safety is a formal item on the agenda between the two leaders. I want to separate the part of this that might produce something real from the part that is being deliberately left alone.

## What the two sides put on the table Sunday

Scott Bessent, the US Treasury Secretary, sat down with Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng in New York on Sunday, and Reuters reported the agenda was AI, trade and critical minerals. CNN Business reported the same day that the American side proposed a notification mechanism between the two governments, meaning a standing channel to flag AI incidents serious enough to reach the level of a national security problem. Bessent described the goal as "moving from opaque to more transparency between the number one and the number two AI powers in the world," and CNBC reported he called the meeting successful. My read is that this is a small thing and I still want it. A notification channel caps nobody's training runs and slows nobody down. It means that when a model does something alarming inside a military system or a power grid, somebody picks up a phone instead of guessing.

## The chips are a different fight

Nothing in Sunday's readout touched export controls, and that is where the money sits. CNBC reported in January that the Trump administration cleared Nvidia to sell H200 accelerators into China with the US government keeping 25 per cent of the revenue, an arrangement with no real precedent I can find. Rest of World reported this week that Nvidia's China business sits near the top of Thursday's agenda, and that the trade has stalled anyway because Beijing objected to the terms. China's leverage runs the other way. Its suspension of the October 2025 controls on **rare earths**, the 17 metals behind the magnets in EV motors, wind turbines, hard drives and guided missiles, expires on November 10, and Beijing can extend it, narrow it or let the full licensing regime snap back.

## Canada is not in that room

We have our own version of this fight, and we are losing the timing on it. The Department of Finance notice says Washington hit $27.6 billion of Canadian goods with 50 per cent tariffs on August 22 under **Section 338**, an old American trade law that lets a president tax a country's exports once he decides it discriminates against US commerce. Ottawa matched dollar for dollar on September 8, at rates of 15, 25 and 50 per cent, across steel, dairy, appliances, farm equipment, pulp and paper and electronics. Carney signed an economic and security agreement with Claudia Sheinbaum in Mexico City on September 18, which reads to me like a hedge against being the odd one out on this continent. Ottawa's CUSMA consultation stays open until November 3.

## The takeaway

November 10 is the date I have circled, and Thursday is not. If you hold Canadian rare earth or magnet names, that expiry will move them more than any summit readout does. If you run a business that ships south, file something in the CUSMA consultation before November 3, because Ottawa is writing its negotiating position right now and one page from you this month beats a complaint in December. I will be watching whether the AI notification channel comes out of Thursday with a name and staff attached, or whether it stays one line in a readout nobody funds.
